Enron, once one of the largest energy companies in the U.S., used complex off-the-books entities to hide billions of dollars in debt while reporting fake profits to investors. When the truth came out in 2001, the stock collapsed almost overnight, employees lost retirement savings that were tied up in Enron stock, and even Enron's outside auditor, Arthur Andersen, was brought down for signing off on the deception. The scandal led directly to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which tightened rules on corporate accounting.

example.scenario: Enron's stock traded around $90 a share in mid-2000. Once the hidden debt and fake profits were exposed in late 2001, the stock fell to under $1 within months, and the company filed for what was then the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history.
example.takeaway: A stock price built on fake numbers can collapse just as fast as the truth comes out.

quiz.question: Why were Enron employees hit especially hard when the company collapsed?
choices: They were legally required to pay back their salaries
Much of their retirement savings was invested in Enron's own stock, which became nearly worthless
The company sued its employees for damages
Employees were forced to buy more company stock every year
quiz.explanation: Many employees had large portions of their 401(k) retirement savings in Enron stock, so the collapse wiped out both their jobs and their savings at once.

terms.name: Startup Fraud (the Theranos Story)
terms.shortDefinition: Misrepresenting what a product or technology can actually do to keep investor money flowing in.
terms.fullExplanation: Not every corporate collapse involves hidden debt — sometimes the fraud is about the product itself. Theranos, a blood-testing startup founded by Elizabeth Holmes, claimed its technology could run hundreds of medical tests from a single finger-prick of blood. In reality, the technology didn't work reliably, and the company used standard lab equipment behind the scenes while hiding that fact from investors, business partners, and patients — some of whom received inaccurate results. The company raised hundreds of millions of dollars before investigative reporting exposed the gap between the claims and the reality, and Holmes was later convicted of fraud.

example.scenario: Theranos raised over $700 million from investors and was once valued at around $9 billion, based largely on claims about technology that could not actually deliver accurate results at scale.
example.takeaway: A big valuation and confident claims don't guarantee a product actually works — investors and companies both got fooled here for years.

quiz.question: What was the core problem at the center of the Theranos collapse?
choices: It failed because of a broader economic recession
Its blood-testing technology didn't actually work as advertised, and the company hid that
It never raised any money from investors
A competitor bought the company and shut it down
quiz.explanation: Unlike an accounting fraud, Theranos's core issue was that the product itself couldn't do what the company claimed.

terms.name: The 2008 Financial Crisis (Lehman Brothers)
terms.shortDefinition: When risky mortgage bets by heavily indebted banks triggered a global recession — Lehman Brothers' collapse was the tipping point.
terms.fullExplanation: In the years before 2008, banks made huge numbers of home loans, including many 'subprime' loans to borrowers unlikely to repay them, then bundled those loans into investments called mortgage-backed securities and sold them worldwide. When U.S. home prices stopped rising and started falling around 2006-2007, defaults spiked and those investments turned out to be worth far less than expected. Lehman Brothers, a major investment bank, was heavily leveraged — meaning it had borrowed far more money than it actually owned — so losses on these mortgage investments wiped out its financial cushion. Unlike some other banks, Lehman didn't get a bailout or a buyer in time, and it filed for bankruptcy in September 2008, the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history. That collapse froze confidence across the financial system and turned a bad situation into a full global recession.

example.scenario: Lehman Brothers held roughly $30 of debt for every $1 of its own capital. That level of leverage meant even a relatively small drop in the value of its mortgage investments was enough to wipe out its entire financial cushion.
example.takeaway: Heavy borrowing (leverage) can turn a moderate loss into a total collapse — small cracks become fatal fast when there's little cushion to absorb them.

quiz.question: What made Lehman Brothers especially vulnerable when mortgage-backed securities lost value?
choices: It had no investments tied to mortgages at all
It was highly leveraged, so a relatively small loss wiped out its capital cushion
It only did business outside the United States
New government regulation forced it to close early
quiz.explanation: Heavy leverage meant Lehman had very little capital cushion, so losses on its mortgage investments were enough to wipe it out entirely.

terms.name: Crypto Exchange Collapse (FTX)
terms.shortDefinition: When a crypto exchange secretly used customer deposits to cover its own losses, then couldn't pay withdrawals.
terms.fullExplanation: FTX was once one of the largest cryptocurrency exchanges in the world, run by Sam Bankman-Fried. Customers believed their deposits were sitting safely on the exchange, ready to withdraw at any time. In reality, FTX had secretly funneled billions of dollars of customer funds to a sister trading firm, Alameda Research, to cover that firm's own risky bets and losses — without customers' knowledge or consent. When rumors spread in November 2022 and customers rushed to withdraw their money, FTX couldn't pay them back, because the money wasn't actually there. FTX filed for bankruptcy within days, and Bankman-Fried was later convicted of fraud.

example.scenario: A customer who believed they had $1,000 sitting safely on FTX tried to withdraw it during the November 2022 panic and found the exchange had frozen withdrawals — much of that money had already been lent out and lost.
example.takeaway: An exchange holding your money isn't the same as a bank account — if customer funds aren't kept separate and safe, they can vanish before you ever try to withdraw.

quiz.question: What was the central problem with FTX, in the simplest terms?
choices: It charged unusually high trading fees
It secretly used customer deposits to cover a sister company's losses instead of keeping customer funds separate and safe
It refused to let anyone buy cryptocurrency
A stock market crash forced it to shut down
quiz.explanation: FTX's core failure was mixing customer deposits with a sister trading firm's risky bets, leaving no real money behind when customers tried to withdraw.

terms.name: Ponzi Scheme (Bernie Madoff)
terms.shortDefinition: A scheme that pays earlier investors with new investors' money, instead of real profits — until the money runs out.
terms.fullExplanation: A Ponzi scheme isn't a real investment at all — it's a shuffle. The person running it takes money from new investors and uses it to pay 'returns' to earlier investors, creating the illusion of steady, reliable profits. Bernie Madoff ran the largest known Ponzi scheme in history, claiming to run an investment fund that delivered smooth, consistent returns for decades. In reality, no real trading was happening — client statements were fabricated, and payouts to existing investors were funded entirely by new deposits. The scheme only works as long as new money coming in exceeds withdrawals going out. When the 2008 financial crisis hit and many investors tried to pull their money out at once, there wasn't enough new money left to cover it, and the scheme collapsed. Madoff's fraud was estimated at around $65 billion and he was sentenced to 150 years in prison.

example.scenario: Someone invests $100,000 with Madoff and is told they earned a steady 10%, or $10,000, that year. In reality, that $10,000 'return' was simply money a new investor had just deposited — no actual investment ever took place.
example.takeaway: A Ponzi scheme's 'returns' aren't profit at all — they're just other people's money, moved around and relabeled.

quiz.question: What makes a Ponzi scheme different from a real investment fund that's simply losing money?
choices: A Ponzi scheme only invests in riskier stocks than normal funds
A Ponzi scheme pays 'returns' using new investors' money instead of real investment profits, and collapses once withdrawals outpace new deposits
A Ponzi scheme only accepts money from banks, never individuals
A Ponzi scheme is technically legal as long as investors are told about it
quiz.explanation: There's no real underlying investment — just new money being used to pay off earlier investors, which only works while enough fresh money keeps coming in.

terms.name: Bank Run (Silicon Valley Bank)
terms.shortDefinition: When enough depositors rush to withdraw their money at once that even a healthy-looking bank runs out of cash.
terms.fullExplanation: Banks don't keep all of their depositors' money sitting in a vault — they lend most of it out or invest it, keeping only a fraction on hand for everyday withdrawals. That works fine as long as only a small share of depositors want their cash back on any given day. Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) had a depositor base concentrated in tech startups and had invested heavily in long-term bonds, which lost value as interest rates rose sharply in 2022-2023. When word spread that SVB might be in trouble, startup founders — many connected through the same investor networks and group chats — rushed to withdraw their funds within days. To cover the withdrawals, SVB had to sell its bonds at a loss, which confirmed the fear and accelerated the run even further. Regulators shut the bank down in March 2023, one of the largest bank failures in U.S. history.

example.scenario: SVB held deposits but kept only a small slice in ready cash, with the rest tied up in long-term bonds. When depositors tried to withdraw about $42 billion in a single day, the bank couldn't turn its assets into cash fast enough and was shut down by regulators the next morning.
example.takeaway: Banks are built on the assumption that not everyone asks for their money back on the same day — a bank run breaks that assumption.

quiz.question: Why can a bank fail during a bank run even if its assets are technically sound long-term?
choices: Because banks are legally required to shut down after any bad news
Because banks only keep a fraction of deposits in ready cash and can't quickly convert everything else into cash to meet a sudden wave of withdrawals
Because bank runs are caused by government shutdowns
Because interest rates always drop to zero during a bank run
quiz.explanation: Banks rely on only needing to cover a small share of withdrawals on any given day — a sudden, concentrated rush breaks that model even if the bank's long-term assets are fundamentally fine.

terms.name: Employer Match & Vesting
terms.shortDefinition: The free money your employer adds to your retirement account — and the rules for when it's really yours.
terms.fullExplanation: Many employers match a portion of what you contribute to your 401(k) — say, 50 cents for every dollar you put in, up to a limit. That match isn't yours free-and-clear the moment it lands, though: vesting is the schedule that decides how much you actually keep if you leave the job early. "Immediate vesting" means it's yours right away; a "3-year cliff" means you get none of it if you leave before year three, then all of it at once.

example.scenario: You contribute $200/month and your employer matches 50% up to $100/month — $1,200/year of free money. But your plan has a 3-year cliff, and you leave after 2 years.
example.takeaway: You'd forfeit the match entirely — always check your plan's vesting schedule before assuming that money is yours.

quiz.question: What does a "3-year cliff" vesting schedule mean?
choices: You get 1/3 of the match each year
You get none of the employer match until you've worked there 3 years, then all of it at once
The match stops after 3 years
You can only withdraw after 3 years
quiz.explanation: A cliff schedule gives you nothing until you cross the cliff, then the full match vests at once.

terms.name: Catch-Up Contributions
terms.shortDefinition: Extra amounts the IRS lets you add to retirement accounts once you turn 50, on top of the normal limit.
terms.fullExplanation: Retirement accounts like 401(k)s and IRAs cap how much you can contribute each year. Once you turn 50, the IRS lets you contribute extra — a "catch-up" — on top of that normal limit, meant to help people who started saving late make up for lost time.

example.scenario: The normal 401(k) limit might be $23,000/year, but at 50+ you could add another $7,500 in catch-up contributions, for $30,500 total.
example.takeaway: If you're 50 or older and can afford it, catch-up contributions are a fast way to close a retirement savings gap.

quiz.question: What is a catch-up contribution?
choices: A penalty for withdrawing early
An extra amount people 50+ are allowed to contribute above the normal annual limit
A one-time bonus from your employer
A tax you pay on old contributions
quiz.explanation: It's an IRS-allowed extra contribution for savers 50 and older, on top of the standard limit.

terms.name: Safe Withdrawal Rate (the 4% Rule)
terms.shortDefinition: A rule of thumb for how much you can spend each year in retirement without running out of money.
terms.fullExplanation: The 4% rule says that if you withdraw about 4% of your retirement savings in your first year, then adjust that amount for inflation each year after, your money should reasonably last 30 years. Flip it around and it gives you a target: you need roughly 25 times your desired annual spending saved up.

example.scenario: You want $60,000/year in retirement income. At the 4% rule, you'd need roughly $60,000 x 25 = $1,500,000 saved.
example.takeaway: Multiplying your desired annual spending by 25 gives you a rough retirement savings target.

quiz.question: Under the 4% rule, roughly how much do you need saved to safely withdraw $40,000/year?

terms.name: Target-Date Fund
terms.shortDefinition: A single fund that automatically shifts from riskier to safer investments as your chosen retirement year approaches.
terms.fullExplanation: A target-date fund is named for a future year, like "2055," and holds a mix of stocks and bonds that automatically becomes more conservative as that year gets closer — heavy on stocks (and growth) decades out, shifting toward bonds (and safety) as retirement nears. It's a "set it and forget it" option for people who don't want to manually rebalance.

example.scenario: A 30-year-old picks a "2060" target-date fund. Today it's 90% stocks; by 2058 it's automatically down to 30% stocks, 70% bonds.
example.takeaway: The fund does the rebalancing for you — you just pick the year closest to when you plan to retire.

quiz.question: What makes a target-date fund shift its mix automatically over time?
choices: Daily stock market news
Getting closer to the year named in the fund
The fund manager's personal predictions
Random rebalancing
quiz.explanation: The fund's glide path is tied to how many years remain until its named target date.

terms.name: Social Security
terms.shortDefinition: A monthly government benefit in retirement, funded by taxes you paid while working.
terms.fullExplanation: Social Security is a U.S. government program that pays a monthly benefit in retirement (or if you become disabled), based on your earnings history and the age you start claiming. Claiming earlier (as young as 62) means a smaller monthly check for life; waiting (up to 70) means a bigger one.

example.scenario: Someone eligible for $2,000/month at their full retirement age would get about $1,400/month by claiming at 62, or about $2,480/month by waiting until 70.
example.takeaway: Claiming later permanently increases your monthly benefit — it's a real trade-off, not free money either way.

quiz.question: What happens to your monthly Social Security benefit if you claim earlier than your full retirement age?
choices: It stays exactly the same
It's permanently reduced
It doubles
You lose eligibility entirely
quiz.explanation: Claiming before full retirement age locks in a smaller monthly check for the rest of your life.

terms.name: Required Minimum Distribution (RMD)
terms.shortDefinition: The minimum amount the IRS forces you to withdraw each year from certain retirement accounts once you reach a set age.
terms.fullExplanation: Traditional 401(k)s and IRAs let your money grow tax-deferred, but the IRS won't let that last forever — starting at a set age (73, under recent rules), you're required to withdraw a minimum amount each year, called an RMD, and pay income tax on it. Roth IRAs are exempt from RMDs during the original owner's lifetime.

example.scenario: At 73, someone with $500,000 in a Traditional IRA might be required to withdraw around $18,900 that year, based on IRS life-expectancy tables.
example.takeaway: Missing an RMD triggers a steep IRS penalty — this is one deadline retirees can't just skip.

quiz.question: Why do Traditional 401(k)s and IRAs have Required Minimum Distributions?
choices: To limit how much you can invest
Because the IRS eventually wants to start collecting tax on money that grew tax-deferred
To fund Social Security
Because the accounts have a maximum balance
quiz.explanation: RMDs make sure the government eventually collects income tax on money that was allowed to grow untaxed for years.

terms.name: Retirement Nest Egg
terms.shortDefinition: The total amount of savings and investments you'll live off once you stop working.
terms.fullExplanation: Your "nest egg" is simply the sum of everything you've saved and invested for retirement — 401(k)s, IRAs, brokerage accounts, and more — added together into one number. Building it comes down to three things you can control: how early you start, how much you contribute, and how it's invested.

example.scenario: Starting at 25 instead of 35 with the same $300/month contribution and 7% return can mean over double the nest egg by 65 — purely from ten extra years of compounding.
example.takeaway: Starting early matters more than almost any other single decision in building a nest egg.

quiz.question: Which factor gives compounding the most time to work in building your nest egg?
choices: How much you earn in your final year of work
Starting to save and invest as early as possible
Checking your balance frequently
Picking the highest-fee fund available
quiz.explanation: The earlier you start, the more years compounding has to work, which tends to matter more than almost any other factor.
